questions.q: What does Wolff suggest about Trump's 2016 campaign?
a: It was never really meant to win, and the victory shocked everyone
It was carefully planned for years by a small inner circle
It expected to win but was unprepared for the transition
It relied almost entirely on traditional television advertising
questions.why: Lesson 1 says staff were already planning their next moves when Trump won.

questions.q: Why did the administration issue so many executive orders?
a: Staff did not know normal policymaking, so Bannon pushed the orders
Congress had passed a law requiring a fixed number each month
Trump preferred orders because they could never be reversed
Advisers believed orders were the best way to win over Congress
questions.why: Lesson 2 says Bannon used orders to create shock and awe around his agenda.

questions.q: Which two camps competed to influence Trump's decisions?
a: The Jarvanka group and the Bannonites
The moderates and the isolationists
The generals and the economists
The campaign veterans and the newcomers
questions.why: Lesson 3 says the persuasion war split between Ivanka and Jared's camp and Bannon's.

questions.q: Why were advisers able to steer Trump so easily?
a: He tended to side with whoever spoke to him last
He trusted only written reports from senior staff
He delegated every decision to a formal cabinet vote
He followed a strict ideological checklist
questions.why: Lesson 3 says his biases let people close to him push the right buttons.

questions.q: How many executive orders did Bannon originally want in the first 100 days?
a: Two hundred, mostly to provoke an uproar
Fifty-five, matching the final first-year total
Twelve, one for each policy area
Five a month over the full four years
questions.why: Lesson 2 says the plan called for 200, though only 55 arrived in 2017.
